context: furnace-led · refractory heat-up & combustion drive the schedule

brief.intro: A glass plant is built around one long-lead centrepiece — the melting furnace — which is built from refractory brick and must be heated up on a slow, controlled curve, often several weeks long, before any glass is made. Everything else — batch house, forming line (float bath or IS machines), annealing lehr, cutting/packing — is scheduled to be mechanically ready by the time furnace heat-up finishes, because once heat-up starts it cannot be paused or rushed without damaging the refractory. That inverts the usual building logic: the furnace refractory build and its controlled heat-up own the critical path, and the fuel/oxygen combustion system's commissioning is a hard gate before heat-up can even begin. Flat glass (float process, using a tin bath) and container glass (IS forming machines) share the same furnace-led logic but diverge downstream at the forming line.

must_get_right: Protect furnace refractory heat-up as an unrippable, uninterruptible activity — once started it runs on its own physics-driven curve and cannot be compressed or paused.
Have the forming line, lehr and downstream systems mechanically complete and cold-tested before heat-up finishes — there is no float between 'furnace ready' and 'glass flowing'.
Treat combustion (fuel/oxygen) system commissioning as a hard prerequisite gate, not a parallel task — heat-up cannot start until it is proven safe.
Sequence batch house and cullet handling to be ready ahead of first charge — an underfed furnace during heat-up or early production risks refractory damage.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and structural steel run a 6-day week; refractory build works a controlled single shift with strict QA hold points — each brick course is inspected before proceeding; furnace heat-up runs a continuous 24-hour calendar for its full multi-week duration once started, since it cannot be paused.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs furnace steel-shell erection → refractory build → dry-out/pre-heat → controlled heat-up → first glass flow → forming-line/lehr hot commissioning → first product to spec. Combustion-system proving is a hard prerequisite gate before heat-up can begin. The forming line and lehr are scheduled to be mechanically complete and cold-commissioned before heat-up finishes, since there is no float once the furnace reaches temperature.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Furnace design — tonnage, fuel type, regenerator vs recuperator — is frozen before refractory ordering; a qualified refractory contractor is engaged for the full build; batch and cullet supply is secured ahead of first charge; and no late change to glass composition or colour that would alter the refractory specification.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Refractory bricklaying needs a dry, dust-controlled, weather-protected enclosure and specialist refractory masons — a scarce, often mobilised-in resource. Heavy lifts — furnace shell sections, tin-bath components — require crane windows before the hall roof closes. Heat-up requires the area secured and non-essential trades cleared for safety.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: refractory QA issues discovered only during heat-up (requiring a costly re-build), combustion-system commissioning delays blocking heat-up start, and forming-line readiness slipping past the heat-up finish date. Contingency is held before heat-up start and before first-product ramp-up rather than spread across erection activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
